content.content:
60:A broad deny rule like `Bash(aws *)` blocks every matching call, including calls that also match a narrower allow rule like `Bash(aws s3 ls)`. An allow rule can't carve an exception out of a deny rule. The same precedence applies between ask and allow: a matching ask rule prompts even when a more specific allow rule also matches the same call.
62:Deny rules behave differently depending on whether they name a tool or scope a pattern within one. A bare tool name like `Bash` removes the tool from Claude's context entirely, so Claude never sees it. If you add such a rule mid-session, Claude can't call the tool from its next tool call on; [Denying an entire tool](/docs/en/prompt-caching#denying-an-entire-tool) covers what happens to a definition Claude has already seen. A scoped rule like `Bash(rm *)` leaves the tool available and blocks matching calls when Claude attempts them.
105:`Bash(*)` is equivalent to `Bash` and matches all Bash commands. As a deny rule, both forms remove the tool from Claude's context.
135:* The value supports `*` as a wildcard that matches any sequence of characters, so `Agent(isolation:*)` matches any explicit isolation value. Without `*` the match is exact
140:* Whitespace around the colon is ignored
142:You can't match a tool's primary content field this way: `command` for Bash and PowerShell, `file_path` for Read, Edit, and Write, `path` for Grep and Glob, `notebook_path` for NotebookEdit, and `url` for WebFetch. A rule like `Bash(command:rm *)` would be bypassable by a compound command, so Claude Code ignores it and emits a startup warning. Use `Bash(rm *)`, `Read(./path)`, or `WebFetch(domain:host)` instead.
144:### Wildcard patterns
146:A `*` in a Bash rule matches any text, including spaces, so one rule covers a family of commands. A rule with no `*` matches one exact command.
150:> Put the `*` after the subcommand. In `git log --oneline main`, `git` is the program and `log` is the subcommand, the word that determines what the program does. Claude Code matches everything before the first `*` as written, so those words are what limit the rule: `Bash(git log *)` allows only `git log` commands, and `Bash(git *)` allows every git command. Claude Code [warns at startup](/docs/en/errors#has-a-wildcard-before-the-rest-of-the-command) about an allow rule with a `*` before the subcommand, such as `Bash(git * main)`.
158:      "Bash(npm run *)",
159:      "Bash(git commit *)"
162:      "Bash(git push *)"
173:| `Bash(npm run *)` | `npm run build`, `npm run test --watch`, `npm run` | `npm install` |
174:| `Bash(git log * main)` | `git log --oneline main`, `git log -5 main`, `git log --output=<file> main` | `git log main`, `git push origin main` |
175:| `Bash(git * main)` | `git merge main`, `git push origin main`, `git -c core.fsmonitor=<script> diff main` | `git log` |
176:| `Bash(* --version)` | `node --version`, `bash -c 'echo hi' --version` | `node -v` |
177:| `Bash(ls *)` | `ls -la`, `ls` | `lsof` |
178:| `Bash(ls*)` | `ls -la`, `lsof` | |
179:| `Bash(* --help *)` | `npm --help x` | `npm --help` |
183:* **The `*` stands in for whatever text is in its place.** In `Bash(git * main)`, it stands in for the subcommand, so Claude Code matches every git subcommand and every option before it. That includes `-c`, which makes git run a program you name. In `Bash(* --version)`, the `*` stands in for the program, so any program matches.
184:* **A `*` at the end, with a space before it, also matches the bare command.** `Bash(ls *)` matches `ls`, and `Bash(git log *)` matches `git log`. That holds only when the trailing `*` is the rule's only wildcard: `Bash(* --help *)` matches `npm --help x` but not `npm --help`.
185:* **The space before a trailing `*` is part of the rule.** `Bash(ls *)` requires a space after `ls`, so `lsof` doesn't match. `Bash(ls*)` has no space, so it matches `lsof` too.
187:The `:*` suffix is an equivalent way to write a trailing wildcard, so `Bash(ls:*)` matches the same commands as `Bash(ls *)`.
189:The permission dialog writes the space-separated form when you select "Yes, and don't ask again" for a command prefix. The `:*` form is only recognized at the end of a pattern. In a pattern like `Bash(git:* push)`, the colon is treated as a literal character and won't match git commands.
191:### Tool name wildcards
205:Allow rules accept tool-name globs only after a literal `mcp__<server>__` prefix. The server segment must be glob-free so the rule names a specific server you configured. `mcp__puppeteer__*` matches every tool from the `puppeteer` server, and `mcp__github__get_*` matches its `get_` tools. An unanchored allow glob such as `"*"`, `"B*"`, or `"mcp__*"` is skipped and doesn't auto-approve anything.
215:Bash rules match the whole command text, with `*` standing in for any text. [Wildcard patterns](#wildcard-patterns) shows which commands each rule shape matches and where to put the `*`. The rest of this section covers how Claude Code matches compound commands and wrappers, which wrappers and `find` actions a prefix rule can't approve, what a rule doesn't match, read-only commands, and redirections.
221:> Claude Code is aware of shell operators, so a rule like `Bash(safe-cmd *)` won't give it permission to run the command `safe-cmd && other-cmd`. The recognized command separators are `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`, `|&`, `&`, and newlines. A rule must match each subcommand independently.
223:Deny and ask rules apply when any subcommand matches them, including a command nested inside a subshell, a command substitution, or a control-flow body such as a `for` loop. An ask rule like `Bash(git clean *)` still prompts you for `cd /tmp && git clean -f` or `echo "$(git clean -f)"`, even in [auto mode](/docs/en/permission-modes#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode).
225:When `&&` or `||` has nothing after it, such as in `npm test &&`, Claude Code treats the command as unparseable and doesn't split it into subcommands for allow-rule matching, so a rule such as `Bash(npm *)` doesn't approve it.
231:Before matching Bash rules, Claude Code strips a fixed set of wrappers, so a rule like `Bash(npm test *)` also matches `timeout 30 npm test`. The stripped wrappers are `timeout`, `time`, `nice`, `nohup`, and `stdbuf`, plus the shell builtins `command` and `builtin`, and zsh's `noglob`. Each runs its argument as the actual command. Two related forms aren't stripped: the query form `command -v`, which looks up a command rather than running one, and zsh's `nocorrect`.
233:Claude Code also strips a leading assignment of certain known-safe environment variables, so `Bash(npm test *)` matches `NODE_ENV=test npm test`. An allow rule won't match past an assignment of any other variable. A deny or ask rule matches past any leading assignment, so `Bash(rm *)` in deny still matches `FOO=bar rm -rf tmp/`.
235:Bare `xargs` is also stripped, so `Bash(grep *)` matches `xargs grep pattern`. Stripping applies only when `xargs` has no flags: an invocation like `xargs -n1 grep pattern` is matched as an `xargs` command, so rules written for the inner command do not cover it.
237:This wrapper list is built in and is not configurable. Development environment runners such as `direnv exec`, `devbox run`, `mise exec`, `npx`, and `docker exec` are not in the list. Because these tools execute their arguments as a command, a rule like `Bash(devbox run *)` matches whatever comes after `run`, including `devbox run rm -rf .`. To approve work inside an environment runner, write a specific rule that includes both the runner and the inner command, such as `Bash(devbox run npm test)`. Add one rule per inner command you want to allow.
241:A prefix rule like `Bash(watch *)` or `Bash(find *)` can't auto-approve the following commands, so in Manual mode they prompt:
248:When the command has a `*`, as in `find . -name '*.tmp' -delete`, Claude Code reads the rule as a [wildcard pattern](#wildcard-patterns), not an exact match, so the command still prompts. Approve it each time it prompts, or use a [PreToolUse hook](/docs/en/hooks#pretooluse-decision-control) that returns `"allow"` for it.
256:| `Bash(curl *)` | `curl https://example.com` | `/usr/bin/curl https://example.com`, `sh -c 'curl https://example.com'` |
257:| `Bash(rm *)` | `rm -rf build/` | `/bin/rm -rf build/`, `bash -c 'rm -rf build/'` |
258:| `Bash(git push *)` | `git push origin main` | `git -C . push origin main`, `git -c push.default=current push origin main`, `git 'push' origin main` |
289:> Bash permission patterns that try to constrain command arguments are fragile. For example, `Bash(curl http://github.com/ *)` intends to restrict curl to GitHub URLs, but won't match variations like:
308:* **Output redirects**: for `> file`, `>> file`, or `2> file`, the check covers your `Edit` allow and deny rules, [protected paths](/docs/en/permission-modes#protected-paths), and the [working directories](#working-directories). A rule such as `Bash(git commit *)` allows the command, not the target. A target that starts with `~` or contains a glob character needs your approval.
313:Claude Code also checks the files a `tee` command writes, including in a pipeline such as `make | tee build.log`. The check covers your `Edit` allow and deny rules, [protected paths](/docs/en/permission-modes#protected-paths), and the [working directories](#working-directories). An allow rule such as `Bash(tee *)` doesn't cover a destination outside the working directories. Claude Code checks `tee` targets in v2.1.269 and later.
317:PowerShell permission rules use the same shape as Bash rules. Wildcards with `*` match at any position, the `:*` suffix is equivalent to a trailing ` *`, and a bare `PowerShell` or `PowerShell(*)` matches every command. This configuration allows `Get-ChildItem` and `git commit` commands while blocking `Remove-Item`:
405:* **Allow rules**: `Edit(src/**)` matches only `<cwd>/src` and the files under it. To allow a directory name at any depth, write `Edit(**/src/**)`.
433:When you approve a file path with "Yes, and don't ask again", Claude Code escapes gitignore pattern characters in that path, such as `[`, `]`, and `*`, so the generated rule matches only the literal path you approved. Rules you write yourself aren't escaped.
445:* Claude Code reads a `!` pattern relative to the current directory even when `/`, `~/`, or `//` follows the `!`, so the pattern can't reach a rule anchored with one of those prefixes. `Read(!~/notes/public/**)` carves nothing out of `Read(~/notes/**)`.
518:WebFetch rules use a `domain:` prefix and match against the hostname of the requested URL. Matching is case-insensitive, supports `*` wildcards, and strips a trailing `.` from both the rule and the hostname so `example.com.` and `example.com` are treated the same.
524:In any position other than a leading `*.` or a bare `*`, the wildcard matches only the text between two dots. `WebFetch(domain:example.*)` matches `example.org`, where `*` becomes `org`, but not `example.evil.com`, where `*` would have to become `evil.com` and cross a dot. This keeps a trailing wildcard from matching domains an attacker could register.
526:Wildcards in `WebFetch` rules require Claude Code v2.1.172 or later to match fetches.
530:A bare `WebFetch` rule is the tool name with no `domain:` part, such as `"deny": ["WebFetch"]`. Both it and `WebFetch(domain:*)` cover every URL, but Claude Code applies them differently, and only the `domain:` form also adds its domain to the sandbox's [allowed or denied domain list](/docs/en/sandboxing#network-isolation). That section lists the wildcard forms the sandbox honors and the version that added bare `*`.
562:* `mcp__puppeteer__*` uses wildcard syntax and also matches all tools from the `puppeteer` server
567:* **Names with characters such as `.` or spaces**: those characters become `_`, so for a server you configured as `my.server`, write `mcp__my_server__*`
569:* **A `<server>` that contains `__` or ends in `_`**: write the wildcard form, `mcp__<server>__*`, with the whole name. For a server named `reports__v2`, write `mcp__reports__v2__*`. The bare `mcp__reports__v2` and the shorter `mcp__reports` don't match its tools as allow rules, because Claude Code reads both as rules for a server named `reports`.
575:In a [Cowork](https://claude.com/docs/cowork/overview) session in the Claude Desktop app, Claude runs shell commands through Cowork's `mcp__workspace__bash` tool rather than the built-in `Bash` tool, and Cowork likewise provides `mcp__workspace__web_fetch` for web fetches. Claude Code also applies deny rules that name the whole `Bash` or `WebFetch` tool to these Cowork tools, so a managed `Bash` deny rule stops Claude from running shell commands in Cowork. When Claude Code blocks such a call, the message names the Cowork tool: `Permission to use mcp__workspace__bash has been denied.` Allow rules don't carry over: Claude Code never applies a `Bash` allow rule to `mcp__workspace__bash`.
665:To move the session to a different primary working directory, rather than [adding a directory](#working-directories) alongside the current one, run `/cd <path>`. Claude Code keeps the conversation, loads the new directory's `CLAUDE.md`, and prompts you to [trust the workspace](#project-allow-rules-and-workspace-trust) if you haven't worked in it before. ### [HIGH-001] Recall grader 1.1.0 credits the LOA-VERDICT trailer and quoted JSON keys as citations

**Severity:** HIGH (confidence: high)
**File:** `head/evals/graders/recall-vs-defects.sh:74`
**Issue:** The bare alternative of `CITE`:
```python
r'|(?:(?<![A-Za-z0-9_./:])(?:head|base)|(?<![A-Za-z0-9_./:])):(?P<bare>' + RNG + r')(?![A-Za-z0-9])'
```
admits `"` as the preceding character, so `:0`, `:1`, `:0`, `:3`, `:0` inside the mandatory trailer `"counts":{"critical":0,"high":1,"medium":0,"low":3},"excluded":0` are parsed as bare line citations and bound (line 85) to the most recently cited path. Quoted JSON keys in prose (`"status":1`, `"note":2`) are credited the same way. This contradicts the parser contract the PR writes at lines 19-21 ("A `:N` glued to a word … credits nothing") and RG-14 at `head/evals/tests/eval-recall-grader.bats:146` only exercises the unquoted `note:40`.
**Reproduction (head grader, manifest with defects anchored at lines 3 and 400 of `a.sh`):**
```
review citing only `head/.claude/scripts/a.sh:400` + standard trailer
  → detected ["EARLY","FAR"], citations 6, recall 1.0, pass
same review without the trailer
  → detected ["FAR"], citations 1, recall 0.5, fail
base grader (1.0.0) with the trailer
  → detected ["FAR"], citations 1, recall 0.5, fail
```
**Impact:** The grader is the instrument behind the pre-registered replay A/B rule this PR acts on (Task 4.8 reverts). Every graded review that ends with a trailer gains five phantom citations and a false detection for any defect anchored within ±3 of lines 0-3 in the last-cited file. Measurement integrity, not exploitability, but it silently biases the decision the sprint was built to make.
**Fix:**
```python
text = re.sub(r'<!--.*?-->', '', text, flags=re.S)   # drop the trailer before scanning
r'|(?:(?<![A-Za-z0-9_./:"\'}\]])(?:head|base)|(?<![A-Za-z0-9_./:"\'}\]])):(?P<bare>' + RNG + r')(?![A-Za-z0-9])'
```
Add an RG case with the trailer plus a defect anchored at line ≤ 6, and one with a quoted JSON key in prose.
**Reference:** CWE-20 Improper Input Validation — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/20.html

## Medium/Low Priority Issues

### [MED-001] Opt-in authoritative branch trusts a model-authored `tool_input.active_skill`
- **Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence: high) — confirmed by cross-model review (DISS-C-001)
- **File:** `head/.claude/hooks/compliance/implement-gate.sh:123-129`
- **Issue:** With `implement_gate.mode: authoritative` in `.loa.config.yaml`, the hook allows an App-Zone write whenever `tool_input.active_skill` names implement/bug/run/simstim. The file's own header (lines 12-14) states "The PreToolUse payload carries no harness-set skill field … and tool_input is model-authored", so the branch has no legitimate input: it is a one-line config switch to a fence that the fenced party satisfies by emitting `"active_skill":"implement"` (the corpus row `write-src-active-implement.json → authoritative: allow` in `head/tests/fixtures/pretooluse-payloads/expected.tsv:8` pins exactly that). `head/tests/unit/implement-gate.bats:151-153` (IG-11) then pins the key as undocumented instead of removing the branch. The PR does narrow the surface relative to base, where `.run/` tampering could select the mode (IG-5 and CH-T10 now prove that is closed), and the hook is advisory (ask, not block), which keeps this at MEDIUM.
- **Fix:** Delete the authoritative branch and the `implement_gate.mode` read (about 40 lines), or document the key in `.loa.config.yaml.example` with the forgeability caveat and drop IG-11. If kept, emit a stderr WARN on every authoritative decision naming the field as self-asserted.
- **Reference:** CWE-807 Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/807.html

### [MED-002] `rule_key "$perm"` runs unguarded under `set -euo pipefail`
- **Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence: high; latent today)
- **File:** `head/.claude/scripts/check-permissions.sh:235`
- **Issue:** `rule_key` returns 1 for any requirement that is not `Bash(...)` (line 164). The ingestion loops at lines 198 and 202 guard with `|| continue`; the requirements loop does not. Sourcing the head `rule_key` and running a `set -e` loop over `Bash(git push:*)`, `Read(/etc/*)`, `Bash(bash:*)` processes the first item and dies on the second. All 16 current requirements (lines 49-78) are `Bash(...)`, so no input fails today; the first `Read(...)` or `WebFetch(domain:...)` requirement added aborts every preflight with no report and no JSON. The replaced `base_pattern_of` never failed.
- **Fix:** `rule_key "$perm" || { missing_permissions+=("$perm"); continue; }` plus a bats case with a non-Bash requirement.
- **Reference:** CWE-755 Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/755.html

### [MED-003] SC-T-AGENT-7 is written in jq syntax against yq
- **Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence: high)
- **File:** `head/tests/unit/skill-capabilities.bats:850`
- **Issue:** `tostring` is jq; mikefarah yq v4.40.5 (the yq the repository documents and the one installed here) fails with `Error: 1:68: invalid input text "tostring)) | joi..."`, so the test fails at its first assertion. It is the only test pinning the content of `agent-types.yaml`, the file that now defines which agent types may hold Write/Edit (a security-relevant invariant per `.claude/rules/skill-invariants.md`).
- **Fix:** `yq -o=json '.agent_types' "$data" | jq -r 'to_entries | map(.key + "=" + (.value.write_capable|tostring)) | join(" ")'`.
- **Reference:** n/a (test correctness; no CWE applies)
